title: What Is the Accessibility Tree?
summary: Understand how browsers build the accessibility tree, compute roles and names, inspect it in DevTools, and test accessible controls with Playwright.
body_markdown:
The accessibility tree is a second representation of a web page that the browser builds from the DOM for assistive technology, keeping each meaningful element’s role, accessible name, state and value while dropping most layout-only wrappers.


You run into it when an audit flags “button has no accessible name,” when a linter complains about a clickable` div` , or when Playwright’s` getByRole` can’t find an element you can see on screen. All three are reporting on the same structure. This article covers how the browser builds that tree, what each node holds, how to inspect it, and how to test against it.


## Key Takeaways


- Browsers build the accessibility tree from the DOM, native HTML semantics and ARIA attributes. Styling-only` div` and` span` elements usually get no node of their own.
- Content hidden with` display: none` ,` visibility: hidden` , the` hidden` attribute or` aria-hidden="true"` is excluded from the accessibility tree, even though it stays in the DOM.
- In simplified form, an element’s accessible name comes from` aria-labelledby` first, then` aria-label` , then native labelling (` <label>` ,` alt` ), then text content, then` title` .
- A` <div>` with a click handler has no button role in the tree, so screen readers don’t announce it as a control and keyboard users can’t reach it.
- Playwright’s` getByRole` locator and ARIA snapshots work from roles and accessible names, so tests written with them fail on the same bugs that block assistive technology users.


## How the Browser Builds the Accessibility Tree


Browsers build the accessibility tree from three inputs: the DOM, the built-in semantics of HTML elements, and any ARIA attributes.[HTML-AAM](https://www.w3.org/TR/html-aam/) defines how each HTML element maps to an accessible role, and[Core-AAM 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/core-aam-1.2/) defines how ARIA roles, states and properties map to platform accessibility APIs.


The mapping from DOM to accessibility tree is not one-to-one. A` <div>` or` <span>` that exists only for flexbox or styling usually gets flattened away. Going the other way, HTML-AAM says that a` <video>` with the` controls` attribute exposes its built-in controls, such as play and volume, as child nodes mapped to roles like button and slider. None of those controls appears in the page’s DOM.


Hidden content is removed too.[WAI-ARIA 1.2 excludes elements from the tree](https://www.w3.org/TR/wai-aria-1.2/#tree_exclusion) when they are not displayed (` display: none` ,` visibility: hidden` , the HTML` hidden` attribute) or carry` aria-hidden="true"` . A “visually hidden” or` sr-only` CSS class is a different case: it moves content off screen, so the content stays in the tree.


## What Does an Accessible Node Contain?


Each node in the accessibility tree exposes up to four things: a **role** (what it is), a **name** (what it’s called), **states** (its current condition) and, for some controls, a **value** . Here is a labelled checkbox:


```text
<  label  ><  input   type  =  "  checkbox  "   checked  >   Email me product updates  </  label  >
```


In Playwright’s ARIA snapshot format, the resulting node looks like this (illustrative):


```text
-   checkbox "Email me product updates" [checked]
```


The role is` checkbox` , the` <label>` supplies the name, and` \[checked\]` is the state. A checkbox communicates its information through its checked state. Value applies to controls such as textboxes and sliders, and the snapshot format puts it after a colon:


```text
-   textbox "Email"  :   ada@example.com
```


For how individual roles are chosen and when to add ARIA roles yourself, see[Understanding Accessibility Roles in HTML](https://blog.openreplay.com/accessibility-roles-html/) .


## How Is the Accessible Name Computed?


In simplified form, a browser takes an element’s accessible name from the first source that provides one:


1. ` aria-labelledby` , pointing at other elements’ text
2. ` aria-label`
3. Native labelling: a` <label>` element, or an image’s` alt` text
4. The element’s own text content, for roles that allow naming from content (buttons, links)
5. The` title` attribute, as a last resort


ARIA beats native labelling. If a button has visible text “Send” and` aria-label="Submit form"` , a screen reader announces “Submit form”, and a voice-control user who says “click Send” may get no match. The full algorithm, including embedded controls and recursion, lives in[Accessible Name and Description Computation 1.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/accname-1.2/) .


## How Do Screen Readers Use the Accessibility Tree?


Screen readers do not read the DOM. They read the accessibility tree through the operating system’s accessibility API, which the browser implements. Core-AAM’s mapping tables cover MSAA with IAccessible2 and UI Automation on Windows, the AX API (NSAccessibility) on macOS, and ATK/AT-SPI on Linux. The screen reader queries those objects for role, name and state, and listens for events such as focus changes. If a property never reaches the tree, the user never hears it.


## How to Inspect the Accessibility Tree


Chrome DevTools and Firefox DevTools both show the accessibility tree directly: Chrome through the Accessibility tab in the Elements panel, Firefox through its Accessibility Inspector.


**Chrome:** open the **Elements** panel, select a node and open the **Accessibility** tab (it may sit behind the More Tabs » button). It shows the computed role, name and properties, plus where the name came from. Turn on **Show accessibility tree** to swap the DOM tree in the Elements panel for the full-page accessibility tree. The[Chrome DevTools accessibility reference](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/accessibility/reference) documents both. Chrome also has an internal` chrome://accessibility` page for browser-level debugging.


**Firefox:** the[Accessibility Inspector](https://firefox-source-docs.mozilla.org/devtools-user/accessibility_inspector/) opens from the page context menu ( **Inspect Accessibility Properties** ) or by right-clicking a node in the Inspector’s HTML pane and choosing **Show Accessibility Properties** . The inspector exposes Gecko’s own accessibility tree rather than information from the platform accessibility layer, so it shows the same output on every operating system.


## Two Bugs the Accessibility Tree Reveals


The accessibility tree makes two common component bugs obvious: a clickable` div` with no button role, and an icon button with no accessible name. Each problem shows up as a missing role or a missing name. Vue and Angular templates produce the same output, because the tree only sees the rendered DOM.


### A Clickable Div With No Button Role


```text
// Before
<  div   className  =  "  btn  "   onClick  =  {save}>Save</  div  >


// After
<  button   type  =  "  button  "   onClick  =  {save}>Save</  button  >
```


```text
# Before (illustrative)
-   text  :   Save
# After
-   button "Save"
```


A` <div>` with a click handler has no button role in the accessibility tree. A screen reader does not announce it as a control, and a keyboard user cannot Tab to it or activate it with Enter or Space. Session replays of this bug show the gap clearly: mouse users click the control without trouble, while keyboard users Tab straight past something that looks like a button but doesn’t exist as one in the tree.


### An Icon Button With No Name


```text
// Before
<  button   onClick  =  {close}><  svg   aria-hidden  =  "  true  "  >{  /* icon */  }</  svg  ></  button  >


// After
<  button   aria-label  =  "  Close dialog  "   onClick  =  {close}>
<  svg   aria-hidden  =  "  true  "  >{  /* icon */  }</  svg  >
</  button  >
```


```text
# Before (illustrative)
-   button
# After
-   button "Close dialog"
```


An icon-only button with no text and no` aria-label` shows up as a button with an empty name, so a screen reader has nothing to announce except “button.”


## Testing the Accessibility Tree With Playwright


[Playwright’s getByRole locator](https://playwright.dev/docs/locators) finds elements by ARIA role, ARIA attributes and accessible name, following the W3C specs, and matches only non-hidden elements by default. A test that finds a control by role and name therefore also checks that the control exposes that role and name.[ARIA snapshots](https://playwright.dev/docs/aria-snapshots) go a step further:` locator.ariaSnapshot()` and` page.ariaSnapshot()` return a YAML view of the accessibility tree, and` expect(locator).toMatchAriaSnapshot()` asserts against it.


```text
import   {   test  ,   expect   }   from   '  @playwright/test  '  ;


test  (  '  save control is a real button  '  ,   async   ({   page   })   =>   {
await   page  .  goto  (  '  /settings  '  );
await   page  .  getByRole  (  '  button  '  , {   name  :   '  Save  '   }).  click  ();
await   expect  (  page  .  locator  (  '  body  '  )).  toMatchAriaSnapshot  (  `  - button "Save"  `  );
await   expect  (  page  .  locator  (  '  body  '  )).  toMatchAriaSnapshot  (  `  - button "Close dialog"  `  );
});
```


Run this against the “before” markup and the` getByRole` call fails, for the same reason a screen reader user gets stuck. A template only has to match part of the tree, and a single-node template like these matches at any depth. If a template lists several nodes at the top level, they must share a parent and appear in the same order as in the tree. When a locator fails, log` await page.ariaSnapshot()` to see what the tree actually contains. These are the JavaScript names, and the other language bindings have equivalents. Playwright’s documentation also says role-based locators do not replace accessibility audits and conformance testing, so treat them as early feedback.


Role and name data matter beyond test runners as well. Some AI-driven automation tools read a page’s semantic structure, which is one reason[agentic browsers](https://blog.openreplay.com/agentic-browsers-introduction/) work best on semantic markup.


## Conclusion


The accessibility tree is the version of your UI that assistive technology actually receives, and a missing role or empty name in it means the control is broken for those users. Open the Accessibility tab on your most-used custom component, check its role and name, and turn that check into a` getByRole` assertion so it stays fixed.


## FAQs


Does adding role='button' to a div fix it in the accessibility tree?


Only partly. Adding role='button' gives the div a button node in the accessibility tree, so screen readers announce it as a button, but it adds no button behaviour. The div still needs tabindex='0' to join the Tab order and a keydown handler that runs the action on Enter and Space. A native button element provides focus and keyboard activation by default.


Does aria-hidden='true' stop keyboard users from focusing an element?


No. aria-hidden='true' removes an element and its descendants from the accessibility tree but has no effect on keyboard focus. A link, button or input inside an aria-hidden container can still receive Tab focus, so keyboard users land on a control that assistive technology cannot name. Setting aria-hidden='false' on a child does not re-expose it. To hide interactive content from everyone, use display: none or the hidden attribute.


How can I read an element's computed role and accessible name in automated tests?


Use automation commands rather than page scripts. The W3C WebDriver spec defines Get Computed Role and Get Computed Label commands, which ChromeDriver implements and WebdriverIO exposes as getComputedRole() and getComputedLabel(). Playwright offers toHaveRole() and toHaveAccessibleName() assertions for a single element, plus ariaSnapshot() for a YAML view of a whole subtree. All of these report the role and name that assistive technology receives.


Why did getByRole name matches change after upgrading to Playwright 1.65?


Playwright 1.65 stopped counting text the browser does not render as part of accessible names and ARIA snapshots. Text that is not assigned to a slot, or that sits directly inside a closed details element, no longer counts. This can change the results of getByRole() with a name option, ariaSnapshot() output and toMatchAriaSnapshot() assertions, so expected names must match only the text the browser actually renders.
